summary.text: Writing the digit sum of \(n\) as \(d\), the congruence \(n\equiv d\pmod 9\) gives \(n=d+9q\); eventual periodicity of powers of \(10\bmod d\) constructs \(n\) distinct positive exponents whose powers sum to a multiple of \(d\), starting with \(d\) congruent powers and repeatedly replacing one power by ten congruent powers to add nine positions without changing the sum modulo \(d\). The resulting number has digit sum exactly \(n\), is divisible by \(d\), and is larger than \(n\), so it is a distinct amicable partner.

full_proof.text:
Let \(D(r)\) denote the sum of the base-10 digits of the nonnegative integer \(r\). We prove that every positive integer \(n\) has a positive integer \(k\ne n\) such that
\[
D(n)\mid k \qquad\text{and}\qquad D(k)\mid n.
\]
It will then follow immediately that the least such \(k\), namely \(a(n)\), exists and is nonzero.

We first record some elementary facts about decimal digit sums.

**Digit-sum facts.** For every positive integer \(r\),
\[
0<D(r)\le r.
\]
Indeed, writing \(r=10s+t\), where \(0\le t<10\), gives
\[
D(r)=D(s)+t.
\]
The inequality \(D(r)\le r\) follows by strong induction: \(s<r\), so \(D(s)\le s\), and hence
\[
D(r)=D(s)+t\le s+t\le 10s+t=r.
\]
For positivity, if \(t>0\), then \(D(r)>0\). If \(t=0\), positivity of \(r\) implies positivity of \(s\), and induction gives \(D(s)>0\), hence again \(D(r)>0\).

We will also use the familiar congruence
\[
D(r)\equiv r\pmod 9.
\]
To see this directly, express \(r\) in decimal as \(r=\sum_j c_j10^j\), with digits \(c_j\). Since \(10^j\equiv1\pmod9\),
\[
r\equiv\sum_j c_j=D(r)\pmod9.
\]

Finally, if \(A\) is a finite set of distinct nonnegative integers, then
\[
D\left(\sum_{x\in A}10^x\right)=|A|. \tag{1}
\]
This is simply the fact that the displayed integer has a digit \(1\) in precisely the positions indexed by \(A\), and zeroes elsewhere. For completeness, it can be proved inductively on \(A\). If \(A\) is empty, both sides are zero. Otherwise let \(a\) be its largest member and put
\[
y=\sum_{x\in A\setminus\{a\}}10^x.
\]
Every exponent occurring in \(y\) is less than \(a\), and therefore
\[
y\le \sum_{i=0}^{a-1}10^i<10^a.
\]
Thus adding \(10^a\) places a new leading digit \(1\) above all the digits of \(y\), with no carry, so
\[
D(10^a+y)=1+D(y).
\]
Induction now gives (1).

The main ingredient is the following construction.

**Construction lemma.** Let \(d>0\) and \(q\ge0\). There is a finite set \(A\) of positive integers such that
\[
|A|=d+9q
\]
and
\[
d\mid\sum_{x\in A}10^x. \tag{2}
\]

We begin by establishing eventual periodicity of powers of \(10\) modulo \(d\). Consider the \(d+1\) residues
\[
10^0,10^1,\ldots,10^d\pmod d.
\]
There are only \(d\) residue classes modulo \(d\), so two of these powers have the same residue. Thus there are integers \(u<v\) such that
\[
10^u\equiv10^v\pmod d.
\]
Set \(\Delta=v-u>0\). If \(e\ge u\), multiplication of the last congruence by \(10^{e-u}\) gives
\[
10^{e+\Delta}\equiv10^e\pmod d. \tag{3}
\]
Iterating (3), for every \(j\ge0\) and every \(e\ge u\),
\[
10^{e+j\Delta}\equiv10^e\pmod d. \tag{4}
\]

We now prove the construction lemma by induction on \(q\), maintaining the slightly stronger condition that every member of \(A\) is at least \(u+1\).

For \(q=0\), take
\[
A_0=\{u+1+\Delta i:0\le i<d\}.
\]
Because \(\Delta>0\), these are \(d\) distinct integers, all at least \(u+1\). By (4), each corresponding power satisfies
\[
10^{u+1+\Delta i}\equiv10^{u+1}\pmod d.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\sum_{x\in A_0}10^x
 \equiv d\,10^{u+1}
 \equiv0\pmod d.
\]
Thus the required set exists when \(q=0\).

Suppose now that \(A\) has already been constructed with
\[
|A|=d+9q,
\qquad x\ge u+1\text{ for every }x\in A,
\qquad \sum_{x\in A}10^x\equiv0\pmod d.
\]
Since \(d>0\), the set \(A\) is nonempty. Let \(m\) be its largest member. Remove \(m\) and replace it by the following ten exponents:
\[
b_i=(m-1)+\Delta(m+1+i),\qquad i=0,1,\ldots,9.
\]
These ten integers are distinct because \(\Delta>0\). Moreover, \(\Delta\ge1\), so
\[
b_i\ge(m-1)+(m+1+i)=2m+i>m.
\]
Thus none of the \(b_i\) belongs to \(A\setminus\{m\}\), and all of them are still at least \(u+1\).

Because \(m\ge u+1\), we have \(m-1\ge u\). Applying (4) with \(e=m-1\) and \(j=m+1+i\) yields
\[
10^{b_i}=10^{(m-1)+\Delta(m+1+i)}\equiv10^{m-1}\pmod d.
\]
Adding these ten congruences gives
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{9}10^{b_i}
 \equiv 10\cdot10^{m-1}
 =10^m\pmod d. \tag{5}
\]
Therefore, if
\[
A'=(A\setminus\{m\})\cup\{b_0,b_1,\ldots,b_9\},
\]
then (5) shows that replacing \(10^m\) by the ten new powers does not change the total modulo \(d\):
\[
\sum_{x\in A'}10^x
\equiv
\sum_{x\in A\setminus\{m\}}10^x+10^m
=
\sum_{x\in A}10^x
\equiv0\pmod d.
\]
The replacement removes one exponent and adds ten, so
\[
|A'|=|A|-1+10=d+9q+9=d+9(q+1).
\]
This proves the induction step and hence the construction lemma.

We now apply the lemma to an arbitrary positive integer \(n\). Put
\[
d=D(n).
\]
By the digit-sum facts, \(d>0\) and \(d\le n\). Also \(n\equiv D(n)=d\pmod9\). Since \(n-d\ge0\), there is therefore a nonnegative integer \(q\) such that
\[
n-d=9q,
\qquad\text{or equivalently}\qquad
n=d+9q. \tag{6}
\]
Apply the construction lemma to this \(d\) and \(q\). We obtain a finite set \(A\) of positive integers such that
\[
|A|=d+9q=n
\]
and
\[
d\mid\sum_{x\in A}10^x.
\]
Define
\[
k=\sum_{x\in A}10^x.
\]
Since every exponent in \(A\) is positive, every summand is at least \(10\). Hence
\[
k\ge10|A|=10n>n. \tag{7}
\]
In particular, \(k>0\) and \(k\ne n\).

The divisibility built into the construction gives
\[
D(n)=d\mid k. \tag{8}
\]
On the other hand, the exponents in \(A\) are distinct, so the digit-sum identity (1), together with \(|A|=n\), gives
\[
D(k)=D\left(\sum_{x\in A}10^x\right)=|A|=n. \tag{9}
\]
It follows at once that
\[
D(k)=n\mid n. \tag{10}
\]
Equations (7), (8), and (10) show that \(k\) is a Harshad amicable partner of \(n\), distinct from \(n\).

Thus, for every positive \(n\), the set of positive Harshad amicable partners distinct from \(n\) is nonempty. By the well-ordering principle it has a least member. This least member is exactly \(a(n)\), and, being positive, it is not zero. Therefore
\[
\boxed{a(n)\ne0\quad\text{for every positive integer }n.}
\]
